p1-economy-context.text: Sri Lanka's economy is recovering from the 2022 economic crisis, with real GDP growing 5% in 2025 and 4.7% in the first half of 2026. Inflation, which exceeded 50% during the crisis, has fallen sharply but has risen again to 8% in August and September 2026. Government revenue has improved, but public debt remains high at around 100% of GDP, while debt repayments continue to put pressure on government finances. Many households are still recovering from the crisis, with poverty remaining above pre-crisis levels. Sri Lanka also faces new pressures from energy prices, global uncertainty and climate-related shocks.

p1-role-context.text: As Finance Minister, your challenge is to balance economic growth, social protection, investment and fiscal discipline. The choices you make will shape Sri Lanka's future growth, debt sustainability and resilience.

p2-brief-1.text: You have nine weeks to shape Sri Lanka's next Budget and help secure the country's economic recovery.

p2-brief-2.text: You are responsible for managing a national budget of around LKR 5 trillion each year and balance spending with revenue, maintain fiscal discipline, and meet critical targets such as a primary surplus and long-term debt sustainability.

p2-brief-3.text: You will not undertake this task alone, but every decision you make will influence Sri Lanka's economic stability and future trajectory.

p3-brief-1.text: Minister, we're counting on you to build a strong team around this Budget.

p3-brief-2.text: We've committed to clear fiscal targets, including improving revenue, maintaining a primary surplus, and managing debt carefully, so keep an eye on the indicators, you don't want things slipping off track. We've set your starting point based on the latest Budget framework, but the choices ahead are yours. And remember, the public will be watching closely.

p3-brief-3.text: One more thing to keep in mind: the IMF programme behind many of these targets ends in March 2027, and the Government has not yet decided whether to seek a successor.

p17-brief-1.text: Before deciding how to spend the money, decide how the Government will raise it. The 2026 Budget focuses on increasing domestic revenue, improving tax collection through the new Revenue Administration Management Information System, and raising tax revenue to more than 15 per cent of gross domestic product over the medium term. The Government has set out a total revenue and grants target of 5,300 billion rupees. How will you raise the money needed to fund your Budget?

p4-brief-1.text: Time to set your spending priorities.

p4-brief-2.text: Education is one of the largest areas of government spending in Sri Lanka, supporting schools, universities, technical and vocational education, teacher salaries, and learning resources. Investing in education strengthens the country's future workforce and economic growth, but increasing funding also places additional pressure on the national budget. Your challenge is to balance these competing priorities when preparing next year's Budget.

p5-brief-2.text: Sri Lanka's health system is recognised for providing free universal healthcare, but maintaining this service is becoming increasingly expensive. Rising demand, workforce pressures, ageing infrastructure, and higher medical costs are placing greater strain on the Budget. Your decisions will determine how much funding the health sector receives and how this affects the country's overall fiscal position.

p6-title.text: Week Three: Welfare and Social Protection

p6-brief-1.text: Government spending in this area supports low-income and vulnerable households through programmes such as Aswesuma. Aswesuma is currently being narrowed: payments to about 425,000 vulnerable households stopped from June 2026, and benefits are now limited to poor and extremely poor families, even as inflation has risen to 8%. Your decisions will determine how much support is provided while balancing government spending, fiscal sustainability, and the needs of those most at risk.

p7-title.text: Week Three: Welfare and Social Protection

p9-brief-1.text: Sri Lanka's defence budget remains one of the largest areas of government expenditure despite the end of the civil conflict. In the 2025 and 2026 Budgets, funding continued to support military personnel, border and maritime security, intelligence, disaster response, and the maintenance of defence infrastructure. While defence spending has remained relatively stable in recent years, there is increasing debate over whether resources should continue at current levels or be redirected towards sectors such as education, health, and economic development.

p10-brief-1.text: Energy spending covers electricity, fuel support, renewables and state-owned utilities. Since the crisis, Sri Lanka has moved towards cost-reflective pricing, and in 2026 the Middle East war disrupted oil shipments and sent prices sharply higher. Between March and May, petrol and diesel prices rose by roughly half and electricity tariffs by about a third, and fuel was rationed, helping push inflation to 8%. The IMF is urging cost-recovery pricing, while households and businesses want targeted relief. Your decisions shape spending, living costs, energy security and the Budget's long-term position.
